# Garden Design Course

Notes from the six-week evening course at the community college, taught by a retired landscape architect called Marion. One session a week, two hours each, with homework that mostly involved measuring things in my own garden.

## Week one: surveying the plot

Start every design with a survey, not a wish list. Measure the boundaries, mark north, and note where water collects after rain. Marion's rule: spend a full year watching a new garden before moving any large plants. Take photos from the same three spots every month so you can see how the light moves. My back garden measured 14 m by 9 m, with the fence on the south side.

## Week two: soil

We did jar tests in class. Fill a jar a third with soil, top up with water, shake, and leave it for a day; the layers show the sand, silt and clay. Mine came out mostly clay. The pH test kit read 6.5, slightly acid, which suits most vegetables. Clay holds nutrients well but drains badly, so the fix is to add organic matter every year and never walk on the beds when they are wet.

## Week three: light and shade

Map sun hours across the garden in midsummer and again in March. Anything under four hours of direct sun counts as shade for planning purposes. The strip along the north fence gets under three hours, so that is where ferns and hostas go, not the vegetables. Trees cast longer shadows than you expect in spring and autumn.

## Week four: paths and structure

The main path should be at least 1.2 m wide so two people can walk side by side or you can push a wheelbarrow without scraping the plants. Secondary paths can be 60 cm. Curves look better than straight lines in a small garden, but only if the path has a reason to curve, like going around a tree or a bench. Gravel is cheap and drains well; bark chips rot down in two or three years and need topping up.

## Week five: planting plans

Plant in groups of three or five, never in single rows along the edge. Repeat a few key plants across the garden so it reads as one design. Put tall plants at the back of a border that is seen from one side, and in the middle of a bed seen from all around. Marion suggested a ratio of roughly one third evergreen to keep the garden from looking empty in winter.

## Week six: water and wildlife

A small pond, even a sunk washing-up bowl, brings in frogs within a season. Leave one corner untidy with a log pile. Water butts on every downpipe. The final homework was a scale drawing of my own garden at 1 to 50, which Marion marked with mostly kind comments and a note that my vegetable beds were too wide to reach the middle of.

## What I am changing

Narrow the vegetable beds to 1.2 m so I can reach the middle from both sides. Move the bench to the corner that gets evening sun. Add a water butt on the shed.
